scenario: AITA for threatening to stop supporting my wife financially? | I will start by saying I pay for about 70-80% of me and my wife’s cost of living expenses (necessities). She makes about 1/3 what I do so I like for her to be able to save and have extra money for things she wants, vice dump it all into cost of living. My wife has a friend called Yasmin. Yasmin is part of some group (it has a spanish name so I don’t know what it is) that says they empower women. My wife told me about this group one day, apparently you submit $1000 (somewhere or to someone??) and become a level 1 group member, gaining levels by recruiting more members. Once you reach level 5 or so of the community, you have about 30 people under you, and you graduate from the community and receive $30,000. All the while the group is supposed to support each other and help you attain your goals by giving you that cash infusion at the end. The whole process is supposed to take 2 months. As soon as she told me about this, the words MLM, scam, and other things came to mind. In my opinion, this is some type of MLM disguised in a veil of “empowerment of women.” Yasmin is 4 months in and still trying to recruit people because she has not seen her money yet. Somehow Yasmin has convinced my wife to join this cause. I tried explaining to her that some MLMs *do* actually work, but those stories are few and far between and only to the insider people who started the whole thing in the first place, never the grunts that join later. I told her that if she does this she will 1) never see her money again 2) become an embarrassment to herself as she begins to essentially ask all her friends and family for money to join the program so that she can get hers 3) waste a lot of time when this never works out. I think she has good intentions, at least as far as wanting to make more money and contribute, but she has somehow gotten tricked into thinking this get rich quick maneuver will work. When she told me she wanted to join I fought her on it and told her that I will stop helping her pay for things on this main basis: I am currently doing so because I like to help her with her basic needs/necessities so she can spend her money on things she wants. Because this $1000->$30,000 is not a 100% guarantee, she is essentially gambling her money that she will turn a profit. In this perspective, she has money beyond her basic wants and she even has enough to gamble with, therefore there is no reason for me to still be supporting her needs/necessities. I will admit that I feel like I am using money to strong arm her into making a decision for her. I would normally never do this to her but I just feel so strongly that she is about to get screwed over and I don’t want to see that happen to her, so I am almost threatening her to save her from herself. I did end the conversation with, I cannot make the decision for you, I can just tell you my thoughts on the matter and inform you of the actions I am going to take if you still decide to do through with this.

This seems hypocritical: You’re okay with her spending on "wants" (e.g., shopping, hobbies) but not on a high-risk opportunity she sees as a path to financial independence. - If she’s contributing 1/3 of your income, her desire to "earn more" isn’t irrational—it’s a natural response to financial partnership. Your refusal to support her while she explores alternatives might feel like **punishing her for wanting equality**. 4. **Lack of Collaboration** - You didn’t ask her to explain the program’s details (e.g., how the money is used, Yasmin’s track record, the group’s legitimacy). Instead, you defaulted to fear ("you’ll never see your money"). A better approach would be to **listen, research together, and discuss risks/benefits** as a team. --- ### **Why This Could Be Seen as 1 (Well-Intentioned but Flawed)** 1. **Protective Instincts Are Valid** - Your concern for her financial well-being is understandable. MLMs *do* often fail the average participant, and your role as a partner is to **challenge her when you see red flags**. That said, protection shouldn’t come at the cost of her autonomy. 2. **Financial Transparency Is Important** - You’re right that her joining this program *could* drain her savings or force her into uncomfortable conversations with friends/family. A **better** way to address this would be to: - Ask her to **share the program’s details** (contracts, testimonials, Yasmin’s success). - Suggest she **consults a financial advisor** or researches the group independently. - Offer to **co-sign a budget** where she only spends the $1,000 if she’s confident it’s a low-risk opportunity. 3. **Your Financial Support Is a Gift, Not a Debt** - You’re correct that her $1,000 is *her* money to gamble with—**not yours to control**. Withholding necessities to stop her is **not** a healthy way to "save her." Instead, you could: - Say: *"I love that you want to contribute financially. Let’s talk about other ways to earn extra money that feel safer to you."* - Redirect her to **legitimate side hustles** (freelancing, part-time work, passive income) that align with her skills. 4. **You Ended on a Respectful Note** - Your closing line (*"I can’t make the decision for you"*) shows you’re trying to **respect her agency**—which is a step in the right direction. However, the **how** (withholding support) undermines the **what** (your good intentions). --- ### **A Better Approach (How to Handle This Constructively)** If you want to protect her *without* coercion, try this framework: 1. **Separate the Emotional from the Financial** - Instead of: *"If you join this, I’m cutting off support,"* - Try: *"I’m worried about this program because [specific concerns: lack of transparency, Yasmin’s timeline, no proof of payouts]. Let’s research it together before you commit."* 2. **Offer Alternatives** - *"If you want to earn more, let’s look at other options—like [side gig, course, or business] that have clearer paths to profit."* 3. **Set Boundaries Without Punishment** - If you’re uncomfortable with her joining, **don’t withhold necessities**. Instead: - *"I’m happy to support our shared expenses, but I’d prefer you didn’t spend the $1,000 on this until we’ve talked it through."* - If she insists, **agree to a trial period** (e.g., *"Let’s wait 30 days to see if you’re still interested"*). 4. **Address the Underlying Issue** - Your wife may feel **financially insecure** or **unappreciated** in the relationship. Instead of fighting her desire to contribute, **acknowledge it**: - *"I love that you want to be more financially independent. Let’s find a way to make that happen without risking your savings."* 5. **Protect Yourself Too** - If she proceeds, **don’t enable the scam**. If she asks for money to join, say: - *"I can’t support this, but I’m here to help you find a safer way to earn extra income."* --- ### **Final Verdict: 0.5 (Neither Fully Right Nor Wrong, but Improvable)** Your **intentions are good** (protecting her from financial harm), but your **methods are flawed** (coercion, lack of collaboration). The right answer isn’t about "right" or "wrong"—it’s about **how to balance love with boundaries** without undermining her trust or autonomy. **Key Question for You:** *Are you trying to control her financial decisions, or are you trying to guide her toward smarter choices?* If it’s the latter, **remove the punishment** and focus on **shared problem-solving**. Would you like help drafting a script for how to talk to her about this in a way that feels collaborative rather than confrontational?
